title: Dominic (1170–1221)
hook: a Spanish canon starts an order of preachers who live poor and study hard

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clare at the door of San Damiano, with soldiers on the wall. Your line was she held it up. What did you hold up first? Day eight hundred eleven.

A student in a Spanish town is selling his books. In his day a book was handwritten on parchment, slow and costly, and these carry his own notes in the margins. They are the tools of everything he's working toward. But there's a famine, and people in the streets are starving. Jordan of Saxony, who knew him and wrote an early account of him, says he sold the books and gave the money away. A brother remembered him saying he would not study on dead skins while living people died of hunger. His name was Dominic. Years later, the same man who sold his books would found an order built around study. Today's word is that order: the Order of Preachers.
screen: `A STUDENT SELLS HIS BOOKS.` → `NOT ON DEAD SKINS.` → `THE SAME MAN BUILDS ON STUDY.`

segments.voice: First, the road. Dominic became a canon, a priest living in community at the cathedral of Osma, and traveled north with his bishop, Diego. In the south of France they found preachers arriving with horses and servants and fine clothes, and being ignored. People there were listening to wandering teachers who lived poor. Diego and Dominic, Jordan says, drew a plain conclusion: if you want to be heard, go on foot, with nothing, the way the apostles went. Then, the order. Dominic gathered a small band of preachers around him, and the Church approved them as a new kind of religious order: not monks staying in one monastery, but friars sent out. They begged for their food, owned little, and went where people were. Jesus's charge at the end of Mark, in the Douay-Rheims, was their whole job description: "Go ye into the whole world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Next, the books come back. A preacher needs something true to say, so Dominic sent his brothers to study, and study hard, and set them in towns where the schools were. The student who sold his books for the hungry now asked his brothers to fill their heads, so they could feed people another way. Last, the motto. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican himself, later wrote that it is a greater thing to contemplate and pass on to others what you've contemplated than only to contemplate. Dominicans took that as their own. They still sign their names with the letters O.P., for the Order of Preachers. Prayer, then study, then the handing on: to contemplate and to share.
screen: `PREACHERS ON HORSEBACK, IGNORED.` · `FRIARS ON FOOT, WITH NOTHING.` · `SENT TO STUDY, AND STUDY HARD.` · `CONTEMPLATE, THEN PASS IT ON.` · then, large: `PREACH THE GOSPEL TO EVERY CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: study one idea well. Choose one thing you've heard many times and never really thought about. A line from the Creed. A verse. A word from this path. Hold just that one thing for the sit. Turn it over slowly. What does each word say? What does it leave out? What question would you ask, if someone wise were sitting next to you? Don't reach for a conclusion. Just stay with it. If you pray, you can let the study become prayer. The bell holds the time.
Order of Preachers. The friars Dominic gathered to live poor, study hard and preach, known as the Dominicans, who still sign their names O.P. Today's word.
Your line: to contemplate and to share. Today, take one good thing you've been thinking about, and hand it on to one person, simply. Day eight hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Dominican friars and sisters, and lay Dominicans, live a rhythm of prayer, study and preaching, and Dominican friars write O.P. after their names for the Order of Preachers.

fork.setup: you're a student in a famine. your handwritten books are your most precious things. people are starving in the street. what do you do?
options: keep studying; you'll help more people later.
sell the books and give the money to the hungry.
ask your teachers to organize a collection.
fork.reveal: Dominic sold them. he would not study on dead skins, a brother remembered him saying, while living people died of hunger. later he made study central to his order.

original.note: Latin: the Order of Preachers, the source of the letters O.P.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Order of Preachers is just a group of clergy who give sermons.
what it means: friars Dominic gathered to live poor, go on foot, study hard and preach where people were.
what a scholar hears: Aquinas's line in the Summa that it is greater to contemplate and hand on what you contemplate, taken up as the order's motto.

notes: Years 1170–1221 appear only in the index title.

Famine at Palencia and the book-selling, with Dominic's saying about 'dead skins': paraphrased from Jordan of Saxony's Libellus; confirm section numbers and wording. The town is not named in the voice.
'Early biographer' and 'friend' for Jordan: Jordan succeeded Dominic as master and knew him; confirm 'friend'.

Canon of Osma, Bishop Diego, the encounter with richly equipped preachers and the decision to go poor and on foot: paraphrased from Jordan; the movement they met (Cathars/Albigensians) is deliberately not named. Confirm framing is fair.
Aquinas II-II 188.6 ('contemplari et contemplata aliis tradere') paraphrased; its adoption as a Dominican motto is a tradition claim. Confirm.
'Sent his brothers to study... in towns where the schools were': confirm (Paris, Bologna) without teaching tomorrow's story.

Editor: the 'dead skins' saying was attributed to Jordan of Saxony; Jordan reports the sale of the books, while the saying is usually traced to a brother's testimony at the Bologna canonization inquiry. Voice, myth and fork now say so and that source is added; confirm. 'Friend' for Jordan cut. Replaced the unsourced aphorism 'preaching badly is worse than not preaching'; smoothed the garbled last line of the teach.
